replays.prompt: My last change made PriceCalculator.reprice in Checkout.java call formatLine for every line item. Did that make reprice and formatLine more expensive? In Jeffrey, "checkout baseline" is before the change and "checkout candidate" after it.

runs.reply:
**Yes. Both methods got more expensive, and allocation went up much more than CPU.**

**What can be compared.** [checkout baseline ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-0245-7724-bb45-1d50ba9f36d6) and [checkout candidate ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-0d8d-7b9f-864a-14d53eeb36bf) were recorded the same way: 30.5 s against 30.5 s, and the sampling settings match on all 93 shared event types. Whether both runs did the same work is not shown. The candidate saw 2,281 HTTP exchanges against 2,381 in the baseline, and Jeffrey can't normalize per request. Neither profile records a commit, so the pairing with your last commit (a9703bf) is your word. The figures come from [the differential on both recordings ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-0d8d-7b9f-864a-14d53eeb36bf/flamegraphs/differential?baseline=01a1c495-0245-7724-bb45-1d50ba9f36d6).

**CPU** (`compare_methods`, `jdk.ExecutionSample`, 3,182 samples against 3,072):

| Method | Baseline | Candidate | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PriceCalculator#reprice` (inclusive) | 233 samples | 435 | +202, about +87%, +6.4% of the profile |
| `PriceCalculator#formatLine` (inclusive) | not present | 181 | new, +5.7% of the profile |

- `formatLine` accounts for most of the growth in `reprice`: 181 of the 202 added samples.
- The callees under `formatLine` are `String.format` and `HashMap.get`.
- `reprice` still spends about 250 samples outside `formatLine` (435 − 181), up from 233 in the baseline. Your diff doesn't touch that part. The 202-sample total is a gross figure for the pair, not a per-call estimate.
- `SessionCache#busyWait` is 2,708 of 3,182 samples, so most of the CPU profile is that busy-wait, not pricing.

**Allocation** (`jdk.ObjectAllocationSample`, by bytes, 15.3 GB against 0.83 GB):

- `reprice` inclusive rose from about 0.62 GB to about 15.1 GB, roughly 24 times as much.
- `formatLine` is new at about 14.6 GB, which is the whole increase (95% of the total allocation).
- The cause is in the source: `formatLine` (`Checkout.java:197-203`) calls `String.format` six times per line and feeds each result back into the next call. The string grows with every pass.
- Garbage collections went from 7 to 43 and safepoints from 11 to 47, which is consistent with that allocation. That is a correlation I didn't trace to `formatLine` specifically.

**Confidence.** The allocation jump is large enough that I'd call it solid. The CPU figures are about 180 samples against a total of about 3,100, so treat them as suggestive: one pair of recordings can't separate a small move from run-to-run variance. This is a CPU and allocation profile, not an end-to-end latency measurement.

Implement fixes: I can propose changes to `PriceCalculator#formatLine` (the repeated `String.format` loop, the source of nearly all the new allocation). Say the word and I'll hand it to `optimize-code`. Both profiles carry no recorded commit, so I can't tie them to HEAD.

replays.prompt: Our database runs far more COUNT queries than the persons service gets count requests. In Jeffrey's "persons dom" profile, where do the extra ones come from?

runs.reply:
In the "persons dom" profile, the 11,141 `count_query` statements come from three call paths. Only one of them is the count endpoint.

| Caller | COUNT queries | Requests behind it |
|---|---|---|
| `PersonController#personCount:89`, the `/persons/count` endpoint | 7,161 | 7,161 requests, one query each |
| `InefficientPersonService#lambda$getRandomPerson$0:38`, probably `GET /persons` | 3,316 | 3,316 GET requests |
| `InefficientPersonService#lambda$getNPersons$0:52`, probably `GET /persons/{count}` | 664 | 664 requests |

The 3,980 extra queries are 3,316 from `getRandomPerson` and 664 from `getNPersons`. All three paths go through `PersonRepository#count:151` and `DatabaseClient#queryLong:181`, which runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person`.

- **Why I think each count is internal:** every path runs exactly one COUNT per trace (`perTraceMax` is 1), so this isn't an N+1 loop. It looks like each service method counts the table before it picks a random person or N persons.
- **How I matched endpoints to callers:** the GET and POST request counts for `/persons` (3,316 and 664) match the other two call sites exactly. The endpoint labels are inferred from those counts, not read from the call sites. I haven't confirmed which controller method sits above each lambda, and I haven't read the source: my attempt to search the repo for `PersonRepository#count` was denied in this session.
- **Cost:** the COUNTs total about 4.4 s of statement time. The 3,980 internal ones account for about 1.7 s of that (3,316 queries at ~1.2 s, 664 at ~0.48 s). They are a large share of the database work, and the ones in the service methods are removable if the count isn't needed.
- **Not checked:** I didn't compare the profile's recorded commit against your checkout.

Profile pages: [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991), [JDBC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991/technologies/jdbc), [HTTP server page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991/technologies/http/overview?mode=server). Example traces: [getRandomPerson path ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991/traces/attributes/search?trace=8033c58925603cd5), [getNPersons path ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991/traces/attributes/search?trace=801f970b5bd5198b).

To confirm and fix this, I'd need read access to the testapp source, specifically `InefficientPersonService` lines 38 and 52. After that, `optimize-code` can propose the change.

The extra COUNTs come from the service layer, not from the count endpoint. I haven't read the source, because this checkout doesn't contain it, so the line numbers below come from the profile only.

Profile: [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991). Its commit is unrecorded (`recordingCommit` is null), so I couldn't compare it with HEAD.

**The numbers**
- The profile has 11,141 `count_query` executions (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person`), about 4.4 s of JDBC time in total.
- `GET /persons/count` was called only 7,161 times. That endpoint accounts for 7,161 of the COUNTs.
- The remaining 3,980 come from two other endpoints, which never ask for a count:

| Call site (from the statement stacks) | COUNTs | Endpoint it serves |
|---|---|---|
| `PersonController#personCount:89` → `PersonRepository#count:151` | 7,161 | `GET /persons/count` (7,161 calls, one COUNT each) |
| `InefficientPersonService#lambda$getRandomPerson$0:38` → `PersonRepository#count:151` | 3,316 | `GET /persons` (3,316 calls, one COUNT each) |
| `InefficientPersonService#lambda$getNPersons$0:52` → `PersonRepository#count:151` | 664 | `GET /persons/{count}` (664 calls, one COUNT each) |

replays.prompt: Requests to the persons service feel slow, but the CPU looks low. Where do the request threads actually spend their time in the "persons dom" profile in Jeffrey?

runs.reply:
Most of the request threads' time in this profile is spent idle, waiting for work. Only about 11% of their samples are inside a request, and the wall-clock graph doesn't show what that 11% is waiting on.

**Where the request threads' time goes** ([wall-clock flamegraph ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1c495-3124-7a57-a220-5d5a975ea991/flamegraph-view?eventType=profiler.WallClockSample&graphMode=PRIMARY&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782&search=org.apache.tomcat.util.threads.TaskThread%5C%24WrappingRunnable), 57,373 wall-clock samples over 76 s):

| Request-thread samples | Count | Share of request-thread samples | Share of all samples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Idle in the pool, parked in `TaskQueue.take` | 10,951 | 88.5% | 19.1% |
| Running a request | 1,411 | 11.4% | 2.5% |

- **Which threads:** the request threads are the 10 Tomcat workers, `http-nio-8080-exec-1` to `-10`. Together they have 12,369 samples, 21.6% of everything sampled. The other 78% is JVM, GC and housekeeping threads plus the Tomcat acceptor and poller, all idle.
- **Inside a request:** the samples go through Tomcat, then the Jeffrey tracing filter `HttpExchangeFilter`, then Spring `DispatcherServlet` and `RequestMappingHandlerAdapter`, then the controller method call. Below that the analyst's threshold pruned the graph. No JDBC, socket, monitor, park or sleep frame appears under any request path. That only means each is under 172 samples (0.3% of all samples), so I can't rule any of them out.

**What this means for your symptom:** low CPU fits workers that are mostly idle, not workers stuck mid-request. The profile does not support "threads blocked on something" as the cause.

Two things could still explain slow requests that this graph can't show. One is that the slow requests are a small fraction of the traffic. The other is that the delay happens before a request reaches a worker, in the connector or in the client. Neither is established here, and I haven't looked at either.

**Other data from the summary:**
- **Lock waits:** the summary lists 586 monitor-enter events, about 672 ms blocked in total. I haven't read them.
- **JDBC:** there are about 15,000 JDBC queries. I haven't looked at their timings.

**Not assessed:**
- What the 11.4% of busy request samples waits on (JDBC, locks, sockets). It needs a lower flamegraph threshold or a per-request trace.
- Time spent before a request reaches a worker.

replays.prompt: Before we scale the persons service up: is the JVM itself healthy? Jeffrey has the "persons dom" profile.

runs.reply:
The JVM's memory management is healthy, but the container is CPU-starved, so that is the thing to settle before you scale. This is the [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0) profile, a 76 s async-profiler recording that includes start-up and shutdown.

| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| GC | Healthy. G1 spent 249 ms of 76 s in pauses (0.33% overhead, 99.67% throughput). The longest pause was 29 ms and there were no full GCs. Young collections free about 235 MB each and leave about 33 MB live. Source: [GC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/garbage-collection). |
| Safepoints | Healthy. There were 7 VM operations totalling 121 ms, the longest 29 ms (`G1PauseRemark`). No thread was slow to reach a safepoint. Source: [VM operations ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/vm-operations). |
| JIT | Fine. There were 11,528 compiles, the code cache is nowhere near full, and 409 deoptimisations across 158 methods, mostly `unstable_if`. That looks like warm-up. Source: [JIT page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/jit-compilation). |
| Threads | Fine. The peak was 29 threads. The 10 Tomcat workers allocate evenly, and there were no virtual threads and no pinning. Source: [threads page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/thread-statistics). |
| Native memory | No leak signal. RSS grew 264 MB to a peak of 866 MB, and there are no direct buffers. NMT was off, so there is no category breakdown. Source: [native memory ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/native-memory). |
| Container | Not healthy (CRITICAL). The CPU limit is 1 core with a 100 ms period. 118 of 301 periods were throttled (39%), which parked the process for 2.7 s. Source: [CPU throttling ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/container/cpu-throttling). |

**What this means for scaling**
- The limiting resource is CPU, not heap or GC. A third of the quota periods were throttled, so more CPU per pod, or more replicas, addresses a real constraint.
- Part of that CPU went to things that won't scale with traffic. The C2 compiler thread (JIT compilation) ran at up to about 30% load, and the "JFR Event Stream 1" thread (the profiler's own event stream) allocated 3.2 GB, far more than any request thread. On a 1-core limit both inflate the throttling.
- Re-measure on a warmed-up pod with the profiler's own overhead excluded before you size the new instances.
- The memory limit is 1 GiB and RSS peaked at 866 MB (about 80%). Live heap is small, but I didn't read the heap sizing or `AlwaysPreTouch`, so I can't say whether that is headroom or a pre-touched heap.

**Not JVM-health, but worth a look before scaling**
- The auto-analysis flagged 131 `Error`s in the minute that Jeffrey's rule reported on, 108 of them `NoSuchMethodError`. That points to a classpath or version mismatch.
- There were 586 monitor-blocked events (about 0.67 s of blocking in total). Contention like that can cap throughput regardless of the number of replicas.
- The process runs as PID 1, which the rules flag as a signal-handling risk.
- The "inverted parallelism" GC warning is explained by the 1-core quota. With 0.33% GC overhead it needs no GC change.

**Not assessed**
- Heap sizing and flags (not read).
- CPU-time samples, native allocation, and security/TLS events were not recorded.

Which of these should I open next?
- `jvm_exceptions` to trace the `NoSuchMethodError` storm (MEDIUM).
- `blocking_overview` to see which locks the 586 monitor blocks came from (MEDIUM).
- `jvm_configuration` and `jvm_flags` to check the heap against the 1 GiB limit (LIGHT).

**Not assessed:** CPU-time samples, native allocation and the security/TLS events weren't recorded. There is no heap dump.

runs.reply:
One lock, `LockPersonService`, accounts for most of the blocking in the [persons lock profile ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-a892-715f-8e72-5848b0e86e5a/blocking-operations). Threads spent 60.1 s blocked on monitors in a 35.6 s recording. That figure sums over 31 request threads, so it can exceed the recording length.

| Lock (monitor class) | Blocked total | Share of blocked time | Blocks | Avg / worst | Threads |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `jeffrey.testapp.server.service.LockPersonService` | 47.7 s | 79% | 2,198 | 21.7 ms / 245 ms | 31 |
| `java.lang.Object` | 8.4 s | 14% | 2,117 | 4.0 ms / 24.9 ms | 31 |
| `int[]` | 2.1 s | 3.5% | 281 | 7.5 ms / 68.8 ms | 30 |
| `AbstractProtocol$RecycledProcessors` (Tomcat) | 0.8 s | 1.4% | 76 | 10.7 ms / 31.8 ms | 30 |
| Everything else (`HashMap`, Jackson `SerializerCache`, others) | about 1.1 s | under 2% | | | |

**How bad it is**
- **Main cause:** `LockPersonService` is a single monitor that all 31 threads queue on. Its 47.7 s is about 1.3 threads blocked on it at any instant, averaged over the recording. It was hit roughly 62 times per second.
- **Worst case:** the single longest wait was 245 ms. That is a 10x tail over the 21.7 ms average, which suggests long hold times, not just frequent short ones.
- **Second lock:** the plain `java.lang.Object` monitor is also hit by all 31 threads, but its waits are short, about 4 ms each. It is probably a private lock object. Which code holds it needs the call paths.
- **Minor locks:** the `int[]` monitor and Tomcat's `RecycledProcessors` are small by comparison. The rest is noise.
- **Waits that aren't contention:** the 21.9 s of waiting on `ReferenceQueue$Lock` is a JVM housekeeping thread sitting idle. I excluded it from the figures above.
- **Caveat:** these are sampled monitor-enter events. JFR only records waits above its threshold, so shorter waits aren't counted and the real totals are somewhat higher. This is medium-confidence evidence.

**Not assessed:** which methods hold `LockPersonService` and for how long. That needs the call-path flamegraph, and I haven't run it.

I found no `LockPersonService` source in this working directory, so I can't offer **Implement fixes** here.

**Open leads**

replays.prompt: Does GET /persons/{count} have an N+1 query problem? Jeffrey has the "persons n-plus-one" profile of this service, and this is its repository.

runs.reply:
**Yes. In the "persons n-plus-one" profile, `GET /persons/{count}` issues one `find_by_id` query per person instead of one query for the whole batch.** Your code is `jeffrey.testapp.`, so I used that as the own-code prefix.

**Caveat on the profile:** it has no recorded commit (`recordingCommit` is null), so I couldn't compare it with HEAD. The source and profile agree on every point below. Still, I can't prove the code is unchanged since the recording.

**The loop in the source**
- `NPlusOnePersonService#getNPersons` (`NPlusOnePersonService.java:43-46`) picks `count` ids and then runs `.map(repository::findById)` over them.
- `PersonRepository#findById` (`PersonRepository.java:111`) runs one `find_by_id` statement through `DatabaseClient#querySingle`. It takes the read lock each time.
- The class comment says the efficient service runs a single `find_all_by_ids` instead.

**What the profile shows**
- The `find_by_id` statement ran 16,492 times, all issued from `PersonRepository#findById:111`. It ran across 3,318 traces, with at most 49 in a single request.
- Some of those come from `GET /persons`, which looks up one random person. The 2,772 calls to that endpoint account for 2,772 queries. The other 13,720 come from `GET /persons/{count}`, which matches the entry-point count the profile gives for that route.
- That is about 24.7 queries per request over 555 requests of `GET /persons/{count}`.
- That route's p95 is about 47 ms, against about 4 ms for `GET /persons` (one query per request) and about 6.5 ms for `GET /persons/count` (also one query per request).
- `code_callSites` reports `repeatedPerTrace: false` for `find_by_id`. That flag is misleading here. The median across all traces is 1 because the single-person endpoint shares the same call site. Filtered to `GET /persons/{count}`, the repetition is clear.

**Not shown:** the profile has no per-call timing for `find_by_id`, so I can't say how much of the 47 ms p95 is the queries themselves. Also, `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion` takes 47% of the CPU samples inside this route. That is a separate cost, but it also runs once per person, so batching the query alone won't remove it.

**Fix:** load all the ids with one `find_all_by_ids` query, as `EfficientPersonService` does. I can make that change with `optimize-code`, or re-profile afterwards with `compare-jfr`. Do you want either?

replays.prompt: Do the requests of the persons service wait on the network or on the disk? The profile is "persons dom" in Jeffrey.

runs.reply:
**Neither, as far as this recording shows.** The "persons dom" requests spend almost no recorded time on sockets or files. The waiting that is visible is in the database statements, and the recording can't tell me whether that's network or disk.

**Network** ([socket I/O page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/socket-io))
- The recording holds 92 socket operations in 76 s, with 6.4 KB read and 112 KB written. The slowest took 31 ms.
- That slowest operation is on port 48090, the same client-side port as one of the slowest HTTP requests. It is the client's connection to the service, not a call to a database host.
- No outbound HTTP or gRPC calls were recorded, so there is nothing downstream of the service to wait on.

**Disk** ([file I/O page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/file-io))
- There are 21 file writes totalling 5.4 KB and no reads. The slowest write took 26 ms.

**Where requests do wait** ([database page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/jdbc))
- All 16,317 statements ran through the `person-repository` group and added up to 6.08 s. That is about 8% of the 76 s recording, summed across threads.
- Statements are mostly fast: p95 is 0.56 ms and p99 is 4.0 ms.
- Only 92 of the 16,317 statements show up as socket events. So the database is probably not reached over a Java socket (an embedded database, for example). I haven't confirmed that, so I can't say whether those 6 s are CPU, lock or disk time.
- Monitor contention adds 0.67 s of blocked time ([blocking page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/blocking-operations)).

**Caveats**
- JFR socket and file events only record operations above a duration threshold. Many short waits would not appear, so this rules out slow I/O but not a large number of tiny waits.
- The slowest HTTP requests ([HTTP page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/http/overview?mode=server)) come in bursts. Several different endpoints hit about 130 ms at the same instant (1793733193357). That looks like a shared pause, such as a lock or GC. It is only a lead. The summary flagged inverted GC parallelism in 5 of 26 collections.

Record it with JFR using the `profile` settings, write the file to an absolute path Jeffrey can open, then import it.

**1. Start the JVM with JFR**

```
-XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile,filename=/absolute/path/persons.jfr,dumponexit=true -Dgit.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
```

- **Why `profile`:** it samples allocations more often than `default` and records shorter lock waits, so short contention shows up.
- **Passing the flag:** use whatever starts the service. That is `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` for a script, `jvmArgs` for Gradle, or `-DargLine=` for Maven tests.
- **The commit property:** `-Dgit.commit` makes the recording name the commit it came from. Note whether `git status --porcelain` prints anything, because a build with uncommitted changes isn't that commit.
- **Where the file goes:** Jeffrey has to be able to open it. If Jeffrey runs in a container, write into a mounted directory.

**2. Drive realistic load for about a minute**

- Warm up first, then record a minute of steady state. A few seconds of samples is just noise with a shape.
- Use the traffic that matches the slowness you're chasing, such as your real endpoints or a load script. A profile of the wrong workload looks like an answer but isn't.

|---|---|

replays.prompt: My JFR recording counts exceptions, but Jeffrey cannot tell me which types were thrown. How should I record the next one?

runs.reply:
Enable `jdk.JavaExceptionThrow` with the throttle off. Neither the `default` nor the `profile` settings give you that.

```
-XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile,filename=/absolute/path/run.jfr,dumponexit=true,jdk.JavaExceptionThrow#enabled=true,jdk.JavaExceptionThrow#throttle=off
```

**What each part does**
- **JDK 21:** the event is off in both `default` and `profile`. That is why you get a count of throwables but no names.
- **JDK 25:** the event is on but throttled, to 300/s under `profile` and 100/s under `default`. The types it names are only a sample, so turn the throttle off if you want every throw.
- **`throttle=off` on a JDK without the throttle (such as 21):** you get a warning that `throttle` doesn't exist, and it is ignored. Every throw is recorded there anyway.
- **JDK version:** you need JDK 17 or later. Your JDK's own `lib/jfr/profile.jfc` shows which behaviour applies.

**Practical notes**
- **Passing the flag:** use whatever the build uses. That is `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` for a script-started app, `jvmArgs` for Gradle, `-DargLine=` for Maven, or `-jvmArgsAppend` for JMH.
- **Overhead:** with the throttle off, an exception storm produces a lot of events and some overhead. Keep the run to about a minute of steady state.
- **Provenance:** add `-Dgit.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)` so the recording names its commit.
- **Location:** write the file somewhere Jeffrey can open, using an absolute path. If Jeffrey runs in a container, use a mounted directory.

Once it's recorded, I can import it with `recordings_analyzeFile` (with `force=true`) and trace each exception type to the code that threw it. I haven't run anything. Tell me which command or workload to profile and I'll run it.

replays.prompt: Some requests to the persons service in the "persons dom" profile in Jeffrey are much slower than the rest. Which endpoints, and why?

runs.reply:
The slow requests aren't tied to particular endpoints. They're slow because the whole process stalls. The container has a 1-CPU quota and is being throttled.

**What the profile shows** ([persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0), `traces_operations`)

| Endpoint | Requests | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /persons/count` | 7161 | 0.35 ms | 2.4 ms | 23 ms |
| `GET /persons` | 3316 | 0.44 ms | 5.7 ms | 30 ms |
| `GET /persons/{count}` | 664 | 1.1 ms | 29 ms | 70 ms |
| `POST /persons` | 664 | 0.84 ms | 29 ms | 77 ms |
| `DELETE /persons/{id}` | 531 | 0.25 ms | 9.2 ms | 33 ms |

`GET /persons/{count}` and `POST /persons` have the worst tails, and every endpoint has a p99 far above its median. Both are write-or-bulk paths, so each request runs more spans (statements, JSON, redaction), which gives a stall more places to land. The slowest 20 `GET /persons/{count}` requests run from 34 ms to 171 ms ([slowest traces ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/operations?operation=GET%20%2Fpersons%2F%7Bcount%7D&kind=SERVER&eventType=jeffrey.HttpServerExchange&tab=slowest)). The slowest 20 `POST /persons` requests run from 38 ms to 175 ms ([slowest traces ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/operations?operation=POST%20%2Fpersons&kind=SERVER&eventType=jeffrey.HttpServerExchange&tab=slowest)).

**Why: the whole process stalls, not one endpoint's code**
- **Slow requests of different endpoints start together.**
  - POST trace `6ad8927daf96cd9c` and GET trace `db3fd1d28109f5b8` started within 7 ms of each other and ran 174 ms and 171 ms.
  - The same pairing repeats at 193358 ms (POST 130 ms, GET 131 ms), at 190876 ms (102 ms each) and at 192205 ms (85 ms each).
  - That is one stall hitting every in-flight request at once.
- **The threads weren't running.**
  - In [trace 6ad8927daf96cd9c ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/attributes/search?trace=6ad8927daf96cd9c), the child span `insert_person` is only 30 ms, but the root has 144 ms of self time.
  - In [trace db3fd1d28109f5b8 ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/attributes/search?trace=db3fd1d28109f5b8) the root has 87 ms of self time.
  - Both exports show the thread off the CPU for about 94% of the request (at least 164 ms and 161 ms), with no I/O, locks, notifications or escaped exceptions.
- **The container is CPU-throttled** ([container page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/container/cpu-throttling)).
  - The quota is 100 ms per 100 ms period, which is 1 core.
  - 118 of 301 periods (39%) were throttled, for 2.7 s of parked time.
  - The throttling counters can't say when it happened or which endpoint caused it. I'm inferring from the matching stall times, so this is medium confidence.
- **Most of the stalls fall in the first 20 s.** The 20 slowest traces of both endpoints start about 7 s to 20 s into the recording, with a few more near 58 s to 63 s. That looks like warm-up (class loading, JIT: 409 deoptimizations) competing for one core, but I didn't confirm that.

**Ruled out**
- **GC:** 0.33% of the recording, longest pause 29 ms ([GC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/garbage-collection)). That is too small to explain 170 ms stalls.
- **Connection pool:** no pending threads, no timeouts, peak 1 active connection of 10 ([pool page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/jdbc-pool)).
- **Slow statements:** the `insert_person` span is 30 ms and `find_all_by_ids` is 37 ms, which are tails but not the stall.

**Side issue**
- **`NoSuchMethodError`:** it was thrown 108 times in about a minute, which is wasteful, but none escaped in the traces I read.

**Not assessed:** I didn't read the population-wide `traces_operationExport`. I read only the two slowest traces, so the per-span cost on typical requests (for example the 36 ms in `person.redact-opinions`) is unmeasured.

**Follow-ups, if you want them:**
- `jvm_threads` against the 1-core limit (MEDIUM), to see whether a few hot threads, or the startup load, exhaust the quota.
- The [exceptions page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/exceptions) (MEDIUM), to trace where the `NoSuchMethodError` comes from.

I didn't offer code fixes. The cause here is the container's CPU quota, not code in this working directory.

runs.reply:
In the "persons dom" profile, the slow requests are not specific to any endpoint. The process stalled, and the endpoints that handle more requests, or take longer per request, got caught more often.

**Which endpoints** (from [traces operations ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/operations)):

| Endpoint | Requests | p50 | p95 | p99 | Max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /persons/{count}` | 664 | 1.1 ms | 29 ms | 70 ms | 171 ms |
| `POST /persons` | 664 | 0.8 ms | 29 ms | 77 ms | 175 ms |
| `DELETE /persons/{id}` | 531 | 0.25 ms | 9.2 ms | 33 ms | 64 ms |
| `GET /persons` | 3316 | 0.44 ms | 5.7 ms | 30 ms | 162 ms |
| `GET /persons/count` | 7161 | 0.35 ms | 2.4 ms | 23 ms | 131 ms |

`GET /persons/{count}` and `POST /persons` have the worst tails, with a p95 about 30 times their median.

**Why:**

- **The slow requests line up across endpoints.** The slowest requests of different endpoints start in the same millisecond and last about as long. At `1793733193358`, `GET /persons/count` (twice), `GET /persons/{count}` and `POST /persons` all started and ran 130 ms each. At `…192205`, four requests started together and ran about 85 ms each. When unrelated endpoints stall together, no endpoint's code is the cause.
- **The slow trace shows the thread was not running.** In the [slowest `GET /persons/{count}` trace ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/attributes/search?trace=db3fd1d28109f5b8) (171 ms), every span is all self time. There are no I/O waits, locks, exceptions or GC pauses in it. Under 10 ms of it was seen running on the CPU, and at least about 161 ms (94%) was not. That is a sampled estimate.
- **The container is CPU-throttled.** The [container page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/container/cpu-throttling) shows a 1-core quota (100 ms per 100 ms period). Jeffrey reports 118 of 301 periods throttled (39%), with 2.7 s of parked time. A throttled process parks every thread at once, which fits the lined-up tails. The throttling counters don't say which request was hit, and I haven't matched the throttled periods to the stall instants.
- **Other causes I ruled out:**
  - GC took 0.33% of the recording, with a longest pause of 29 ms ([GC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/garbage-collection)). That cannot produce 130–175 ms stalls.
  - Safepoints add nothing beyond the GC pauses (longest 29 ms).
  - The JDBC pool never ran short: average 0.04 connections active, no threads waiting, no timeouts ([pool page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/jdbc-pool)).

**Why those two endpoints rank worst** is my inference, not a measurement. `POST /persons` writes, and `GET /persons/{count}` does a batch lookup plus per-person processing (`person.redact-opinions` took 36 ms in that slow trace). Both therefore hold the CPU longer per request and are more likely to be mid-request when the quota runs out.

**Not checked:**

- **Contended monitors:** 11 of them blocked threads for 672 ms in total. I didn't see which lock it was ([lock contention ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/blocking-operations)), so I can't say whether it adds to the stalls.
- **Exceptions:** the profile logged 131 errors, mostly `NoSuchMethodError`, which is a separate matter from latency.
- **Source code:** this working directory doesn't hold the persons service, so I mapped nothing to code.

**Next, if you want it:**
- Match the throttled periods to the stall instants with `jvm_threads` and the per-thread CPU load (MEDIUM). That would confirm the quota as the cause.
- Check which monitor was contended with `blocking_monitors` (MEDIUM).

In "persons dom", the slow requests are `GET /persons/{count}` and `POST /persons`, with `DELETE /persons/{id}` a smaller third. Their code is not the main cause. The slowest requests of unrelated endpoints stall at the same instants, which points to the container's CPU quota. The traces don't prove that link, though.

**Which endpoints** (from [traces operations ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/operations))

| Endpoint | Requests | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`GET /persons/{count}` ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/operations?operation=GET%20%2Fpersons%2F%7Bcount%7D&kind=SERVER&eventType=jeffrey.HttpServerExchange) | 664 | 1.1 ms | 29 ms | 70 ms |
| [`POST /persons` ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/operations?operation=POST%20%2Fpersons&kind=SERVER&eventType=jeffrey.HttpServerExchange) | 664 | 0.84 ms | 29 ms | 77 ms |

| `GET /persons` | 3,316 | 0.44 ms | 5.7 ms | 30 ms |
| `GET /persons/count` | 7,161 | 0.35 ms | 2.4 ms | 23 ms |

The read-only list and count endpoints are the fast ones. The two slow endpoints each have about 660 requests, and the DELETE endpoint has 531.

**Why they look slow**

1. **What a slow trace contains.** The slowest [`GET /persons/{count}` trace ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/attributes/search?trace=db3fd1d28109f5b8) took 171 ms. Its spans account for only a small part of that:
   - `find_all_by_ids` took 37 ms and `person.redact-opinions` took 36 ms. Both are on the critical path.
   - The root span has 87 ms of self time. Fewer than 10 ms of that was on-CPU samples.
   - The slowest [`POST /persons` trace ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/traces/attributes/search?trace=6ad8927daf96cd9c) took 174 ms. `insert_person` took 30 ms, and the root has 144 ms of self time.
   - In both, at least 94% of the time was spent with the thread not seen running. There were no socket or file waits, no notifications, and no escaped exceptions.

2. **The slow requests line up in time.** The slowest requests of both endpoints start within a few milliseconds of each other:
   - 187,590 vs 187,597 ms
   - 193,358 vs 193,358 ms
   - 190,876 vs 190,876 ms
   - 192,205 vs 192,205 ms
   - 195,300 vs 195,300 ms

   Requests of different endpoints that start together and last about as long mean every thread stalled at once.

3. **A process-wide cause fits.** [`jvm_container` ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/container/cpu-throttling) reports a CRITICAL finding:
   - The CPU quota is 1 core (100 ms per 100 ms period).
   - 118 of 301 CFS periods were throttled (39%), for 2,739 ms of parked time.
   - Throttling parks all threads, so it fits the pattern in points 1 and 2.
   - The counters can't say which request was parked or when. I'm inferring the link from the matching stalls, so treat it as likely, not proven.

**Ruled out**
- **GC:** collections took 0.33% of the recording, and the longest pause was 29 ms ([GC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/garbage-collection)). That is too short and too rare to explain 100–170 ms stalls across many requests.
- **Connection pool:** the pool never had a waiting thread or a timeout, and the average number of active connections was 0.04 ([pool page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/jdbc-pool)).
- **Slow statements:** `insert_person` and `find_all_by_ids` are tens of milliseconds at most.

**Possible contributors I haven't separated out**
- All five paired stalls fall in the first ~10–20 s of the recording, with a few more later around 238–243 s. Early on, JIT warm-up could add to the quota pressure.
- The profile also shows 586 monitor-blocked events (about 672 ms of blocking in total) and 409 deoptimisations. I haven't checked whether either one overlaps the slow requests.
- This slice is probably a poor stand-in for `GET /persons/{count}` and `POST /persons`. The writes and the `{count}` read do the most work per request, so they are the most likely to run out of quota.

**Next step, your pick:**
- [`jvm_threads`](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/thread-statistics) shows per-thread CPU load against the 1-core limit, to see whether the quota is simply too low.
- `jvm_jit` plus a time-window check would show whether the early stalls are warm-up.
- The lock-contention view would show whether the 586 monitor-blocked events overlap the slow requests.

| 3 | `count_query` (inside `person.pick-ids`) | `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person` runs on every request, via `PersonRepository#count` and `DatabaseClient#queryLong`. | `InefficientPersonService.java:52` |
| 4 | `find_all_by_ids` | A single `SELECT * FROM person WHERE id IN (:ids)` through `PersonRepository#findByIds`, not one query per person. | `PersonRepository.java:132` |

I could rank the hotspots from the [persons dom profile ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0), but I couldn't read the source. Everything below comes from the profile alone, so I haven't confirmed any of it against code. Each proposed change is a hypothesis to check once `jeffrey.testapp.server` is checked out.

## Summary

- **Commit:** the recording has no commit (`recordingCommit` is null), so I can't say which revision it measured.
- **What I read:** CPU, wall-clock and lock contention, ranked by `jeffrey.testapp.server.` code.
- **Where the CPU goes:** only 29% of CPU samples land in the app's own code, and most of that is database access.
- **Wall-clock:** the app's code accounts for only 1.8% of non-idle samples. Most of the time is spent in framework code or waiting, not in the app's own methods.
- **Locks:** these are negligible, at 672 ms blocked in total over a 76 s recording. I wouldn't spend effort there.
- **Not assessed:** the database (`jdbc_overview`), traces and the exceptions page. The profile flags 108 `NoSuchMethodError`s and the JDBC statements, and I haven't looked at either.

## Code findings (hypotheses, source not read)

### PersonRepository#count → DatabaseClient#queryLong
- **Cost:** `count` is 14% of CPU inclusive (716 of 5097 samples). 636 of those samples (12.5%) are in the `NamedParameterJdbcTemplate#queryForObject` call at `DatabaseClient` line 182. It is the largest single app cost on CPU, and the top app-side wall-clock frame too.
- **Callers:** `PersonController#personCount`, and `InefficientPersonService#getRandomPerson`.
- **Proposed change:** check what the count query does. If it's a full `COUNT(*)` run on every request, cache the value with a short TTL or maintain it incrementally. Also check for a missing index.
- **Confidence:** medium. The share is measured, but the cause is unverified.

### InefficientPersonService#getNPersons / getRandomPerson → PersonRepository#findById, findByIds
- **N+1 shape:** the class name suggests deliberate inefficiency. `findById` shows up as a caller of `query` and `paramSourceToJson`, and the profile holds 15,122 JDBC queries against 12,348 HTTP exchanges.
- **Proposed change:** if `getNPersons` loops over `findById`, replace it with a single `findByIds` (`WHERE id IN (...)`) call.
- **Check first:** run `code_callSites` and look at `repeatedPerTrace`. I haven't, so this is unconfirmed.
- **Confidence:** low to medium.

### DatabaseClient#paramSourceToJson
- **Cost:** about 0.5% of CPU. 23 of its 26 samples are in Jackson's `JsonNode#toString`, at line 242.
- **Proposed change:** it appears to serialise the parameters to JSON on every query, probably for the trace events. Build that string only when tracing is enabled, or lazily.
- **Confidence:** medium on the cause, low on the gain, since the share is small.

### PersonRepository#modifyOpinion
- **Cost:** about 0.6% of CPU. Line 350 calls `String#replaceAll`, which compiles the regex on every call.
- **Proposed change:** precompile the `Pattern` as a static constant, or use `String#replace` if the pattern is a plain literal.
- **Confidence:** medium. The gain is small but the change is safe.

### PersonController#personCount / getRandomPerson
- **Cost:** about 0.4% of CPU and 0.4–0.5% of wall-clock, mostly in `Logger#info` at lines 49 and 90.
- **Proposed change:** lower the log level for these messages, or check that the appender isn't synchronous or doing slow I/O.
- **Confidence:** low.

## Configuration findings

- **Hikari:** `getString` on the result set shows lock time. The amount is small, but it's worth checking the pool size with `jdbc_pools`, which I haven't called.
- **GC:** the auto-analysis flags inverted parallelism in 5 of 26 collections. This points at too few CPUs for the GC threads, or a container limit.

## Not located

- `ServerApplication#main` (8.8% of CPU) is Spring Boot startup, not request work.
- `TracedEvents#emit` is Jeffrey's own instrumentation inside `DatabaseClient`. Its cost isn't from the app.

## Next steps

1. Check out `jeffrey.testapp.server` at the commit the recording came from, which is unknown. Then I can read `PersonRepository`, `DatabaseClient` and `InefficientPersonService`, confirm or drop each finding, and propose real edits.
2. Meanwhile I can run `code_callSites` and `jdbc_overview` against the profile to confirm the N+1 and see which statements dominate. Do you want me to?

Write that up as a short report for my team.

runs.reply:
# Report: "persons dom" vs "persons direct"

Your two claims came out differently. The extra COUNT queries are confirmed, but the cost of the first claim was about 1.2 s only for one endpoint. The second claim is not supported as you wrote it: the allocation increase is real, but almost none of it comes from building the JSON tree.

**Profiles:** primary is `persons dom` (`01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0`, 76.09 s). The baseline is `persons direct` (`01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a`, 76.09 s). I assumed "direct" is the baseline, so please confirm. The two runs are the same length and had 12,348 and 12,349 HTTP server events.

## 1. Extra COUNT queries: confirmed, 1.2 s for one endpoint and 1.7 s for two

**Symptom:** `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person` runs far more often in "dom" than in "direct".

**Evidence:**
- `jdbc_overview` on both profiles gives `count_query` 11,141 executions in dom against 7,163 in direct. That is 3,978 more.
- `code_callSites eventType=jeffrey.JdbcQuery filterField=name filterValue=count_query` on dom splits the 11,141 into three call sites:

| Call site | Executions | Total time |
|---|---|---|
| `PersonController#personCount:89` | 7,161 | 2.72 s |
| `InefficientPersonService#lambda$getRandomPerson$0:38` | 3,316 | 1,215,524,866 ns = 1.22 s |
| `InefficientPersonService#lambda$getNPersons$0:52` | 664 | 483,467,759 ns = 0.48 s |

- All three go through `PersonRepository#count:151`. Each is issued once per request (`perTraceMax` 1, `repeatedPerTrace` false).

**Interpretation:**
- The 7,161 from `personCount` match the baseline's 7,163 closely, so they look like the endpoint's own work. That is an inference, because I did not run `code_callSites` on the baseline.
- The extra ~3,980 executions are the two `InefficientPersonService` call sites, which match the 3,978 difference.
- The 1.2 s you quoted is `getRandomPerson` alone. With `getNPersons` the extra COUNT time is **1.70 s** (3,980 executions). I did not check which URL maps to each method, so I can't confirm "every GET /persons".
- Whole-group JDBC time went from 3.62 s to 6.08 s. That is 2.46 s more, so COUNT is not the only thing that grew. I did not break out the rest.
- Time is summed over concurrent requests. It is not a share of wall clock.

**Recommendation:** none yet. I have not opened `InefficientPersonService`, `PersonRepository` or `DatabaseClient#queryLong`, so I have no lines to point to. The call paths suggest removing the `count()` call at `InefficientPersonService.java:38` and `:52`, but that is a hypothesis to check in source. After any change, re-profile and compare `count_query` counts.

**Confidence:** high on counts and time for the dom profile. Medium on the split into extra versus pre-existing, because the baseline call sites were not read.

**Link:** [JDBC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/jdbc)

## 2. Allocation up about 26%: real, but it is not the JSON tree

**Symptom:** the dom run allocated more.

**Evidence:**
- `memory_allocations`: 4,099,353,541 bytes in dom against 3,240,636,988 bytes in direct, on `jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB`. The difference is 858.7 MB, or +26.5% (my arithmetic).
- `compare_movements eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB useWeight=true` reports 3.8 GiB against 3.0 GiB, with `baseline_scale_factor` 1.000 and no comparability problems.
- The largest movers are mostly not application code:
  - `byte[]` +379.3 MiB, from `Matcher#appendReplacement` and `StringBuilder`.
  - `ArrayList$Itr` +188.5 MiB, from `jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedObject#getValue`.
  - `String` +87.0 MiB, from `String#split`.
  - `char[]` +65.0 MiB, from `jdk.jfr.internal.tool.StructuredWriter#flush`.
  - Several others come from `PrettyWriter`.
- The only JSON-tree entry is `LinkedHashMap$Entry` at +8.0 MiB, from `tools.jackson.databind.node.ObjectNode#put`. That is about 1% of the 818.9 MiB difference.
- `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion` shows up as `int[]` +14.0 MiB, from `String#replaceAll` compiling a regex.

**Interpretation:**
- The growth is not mainly JSON-tree building.
- Much of it sits in `jdk.jfr` consumer and printing frames. Those are the recording tooling's own work (the auto-analysis also names thread "JFR Event Stream 1"), so they say nothing about the service.
- I have not separated service allocation from tooling allocation for the whole 858 MB.
- I would not put "a quarter more, from the JSON tree" in front of the team.

# Report: `persons dom` vs `persons direct`, extra COUNT and higher allocation

I re-read both figures from Jeffrey before writing them down. The COUNT cost holds up, with a split you should know about. The allocation total holds up, but the data doesn't support blaming it on the JSON tree.

I compared `persons dom` (primary) against `persons direct` as the baseline. You didn't name a baseline, so I picked it because both were recorded at the same moment and are the same length. Tell me if you meant a different one.

## 1. Extra `SELECT COUNT(*)` on the GET person lookups

**Symptom:** The dom profile issues 3,980 more COUNT statements than the baseline. The 1.2 s you quoted matches only one of the two GET endpoints.

**Evidence:**
- `jdbc_overview` on dom: `count_query` ran 11,141 times. On the baseline it ran 7,163 times. All other statement counts are the same, so the two runs did the same amount of work: `find_by_id` ran 3,316 vs 3,320 times and `find_all_by_ids` 664 vs 664.
- `code_callSites eventType=jeffrey.JdbcQuery groupBy=name` on dom splits the COUNTs by caller:

| Caller | Count | Total time | Mean | Max per request |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `InefficientPersonService#getRandomPerson` (`PersonRepository#count:151`) | 3,316 | 1,215,524,866 ns (1.22 s) | 367 µs | 1 |
| `InefficientPersonService#getNPersons` (`PersonRepository#count:151`) | 664 | 483,467,759 ns (0.48 s) | 728 µs | 1 |
| `PersonController#personCount` | 7,161 | 2,724,558,919 ns (2.72 s) | 380 µs | 1 |

- The `personCount` calls match the baseline's 7,163 COUNTs. They come from a separate endpoint, so they are not extra.

**Interpretation:**
- The extra COUNTs total 1.70 s: 1.22 s from the random-person lookup, which is your 1.2 s, plus 0.48 s from the N-persons lookup.
- This is statement time summed over threads, over a 76.09 s recording. It is not wall-clock time.
- The whole `person-repository` group went from 3,616,495,449 ns to 6,080,641,833 ns, which is +2.46 s. Not all of that is COUNT. Other statements also got slower, for example the delete p99 went from 2.9 ms to 18.1 ms. I haven't looked into why.
- Each COUNT runs once per request, so this is not an N+1 pattern.
- I haven't read the source, so "before it looks the person up" is your description, not something I checked.

**Recommendation:** Remove or defer the `PersonRepository#count` call at `PersonRepository.java:151` on both service paths (`jeffrey.testapp.server.service.InefficientPersonService`). Check afterwards that `count_query` drops back to about 7,163 in a re-profile. — apply with *Implement fixes*

**Confidence:** High. It's a direct measurement, and the baseline's statement counts cross-check it.

**Link:** [JDBC page ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/technologies/jdbc)

## 2. Allocation is about a quarter higher, but not because of the JSON tree

**Symptom:** The dom run allocates 26.5% more than the baseline.

**Evidence:**
- `memory_allocations` on dom: 4,099,353,541 bytes. Baseline: 3,240,636,988 bytes. That is +858,716,553 bytes.
- `compare_movements eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB useWeight=true` reports no comparability problems, with run lengths 76.09 s vs 76.09 s.
- The largest movers are `byte[]` (+379 MiB), `ArrayList$Itr` (+188 MiB), `String` (+87 MiB) and `char[]` (+65 MiB).
- The example paths for these run through `jdk.jfr.consumer.*`, `jdk.jfr.internal.tool.PrettyWriter` and `String#split`, not through the person endpoints.
- The Jackson `ObjectNode` path shows only `LinkedHashMap$Entry` at +8 MiB. That is about 1% of the +858 MB.
- The two person-service frames moved by roughly +6.5 MiB (`getNPersons`, 184 vs 178.5 MiB) and +6.5 MiB (`getRandomPerson`, 61 vs 54.5 MiB).

**Interpretation:**
- The +26.5% total is real in this pair of recordings. Attributing it to JSON tree building is not supported.
- Most of the added bytes sit in JFR-reading frames. That suggests the recording captured allocation from JFR processing in the same JVM, or from something else not tied to the endpoints. I haven't confirmed which.
- Allocation events are samples, so every share here is an estimate.
- There is no repetition, so a single pair can't separate a real move from run-to-run variance.

**Recommendation:** None yet. Run `compare_flamegraph` on allocation scoped to `jeffrey.testapp.*` frames, or re-record with the JFR-reading work kept out of the process, then check the dom builder's cost on its own. I'd drop the "JSON tree" wording until that is measured.

**Confidence:** High for the total. Low for the JSON-tree attribution.

# Report: "persons dom" vs "persons direct": extra COUNT query and allocation

I read each of your figures back from Jeffrey. The COUNT finding holds, with a correction to the 1.2 s. The allocation finding holds as a number, but the profile doesn't support blaming the JSON tree.

**Setup.** The primary is [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0) (`01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0`, 76.09 s, async-profiler). I assumed the baseline is [persons direct ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a) (`01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a`, 76.09 s), because it was recorded at the same moment. Tell me if you meant a different baseline. `compare_movements` reports no comparability problems for the pair.

## 1. Extra `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person` before the lookup

**Symptom.** The dom run issues far more COUNT statements than the direct run.

**Evidence.**
- `jdbc_overview` on both profiles: `count_query` runs 11,141 times in dom against 7,163 in direct, which is 3,978 more.
- `code_callSites eventType=jeffrey.JdbcQuery groupBy=name` on dom splits the 11,141 by caller (`PersonRepository#count:151`):

| Caller | Count | Total time | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PersonController#personCount:89` | 7,161 | 2,724.6 ms | 0.38 ms |
| `InefficientPersonService#getRandomPerson` (lambda, line 38) | 3,316 | 1,215.5 ms | 0.37 ms |
| `InefficientPersonService#getNPersons` (lambda, line 52) | 664 | 483.5 ms | 0.73 ms |

**Interpretation.**
- The 7,161 `personCount` calls match direct's 7,163 total, so I take them as the existing baseline traffic. I did not read direct's call sites, so this is an inference.
- The extra ~3,980 COUNTs come from `getRandomPerson` and `getNPersons`. Each of those requests issues exactly one (`perTraceMax` = 1), so this is not an N+1.
- Your 1.2 s matches only the `getRandomPerson` site (1,215.5 ms). Adding the `getNPersons` site makes it **1,699 ms** of COUNT time in total.
- That time is summed over request threads, so it is not a share of the 76 s wall clock.
- I did not check that the `getRandomPerson` and `getNPersons` endpoints are what you call "GET /persons". The profile only names the service methods.

**Recommendation.** Drop or cache the COUNT at `PersonRepository#count` (line 151) on these two paths. I have not opened the source, so this names a frame, not a fix. Verify by re-profiling and checking that `count_query` falls back to about 7,160.

**Confidence.** Medium to high. The counts are direct measurements, but the baseline split is inferred.

## 2. About a quarter more allocation

**Symptom.** The dom run allocates more.

**Evidence.**
- `memory_allocations` / `compare_list` on `jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB`: 4,099,353,541 B in dom against 3,240,636,988 B in direct, which is **+26.5%** over equal-length runs.
- `compare_movements useWeight=true` ranks the movers by self weight:

| Type | Change | Example path (largest single contributor) |
|---|---|---|
| `byte[]` | +379 MiB | `Matcher#appendReplacement` |
| `ArrayList$Itr` | +188.5 MiB | `jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedObject#getValue` |
| `String` | +87 MiB | `String#split` |
| `char[]` | +65 MiB | `jdk.jfr.internal.tool.StructuredWriter#flush` |
| Jackson `ObjectNode` → `LinkedHashMap$Entry` | **+8 MiB** | `ObjectNode#put` |

- The candidate-rename pairs show the service methods themselves are close: `getNPersons` 184 MiB (Inefficient) against 178.5 MiB (Efficient), and `getRandomPerson` 61 against 54.5 MiB.

**Interpretation.**
- The +26.5% is real.
- The profile does not support attributing it to JSON tree building. The Jackson node type grew by roughly 8 MiB out of about 820 MiB of net growth.
- Most of the biggest movers have example paths inside `jdk.jfr.*`, which is JFR's own parsing and printing machinery, not the service. Those are the biggest single paths, not the whole story, so I can't rule out other contributions.
- The tree-building claim stays a hypothesis until someone looks at the allocation flamegraph under the controller.

**Recommendation.** None yet. To test it, run `flamegraph_export eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB useWeight=true` scoped to `PersonController`. Then re-record both runs with the JFR event-stream consumer excluded.

**Confidence.** High for the +26.5% figure. Low for the cause. This is a single pair of recordings with no variance estimate, and allocation is sampled.

- **Sampler loss and sampling settings.** I did not run `compare_quality` on this pair.
- **Latency.** I did not run `traces_operations` or `http_overview`, so I can't say how much the extra COUNT, or the allocation, costs per request.
- **Source.** I have not read the repository's `PersonRepository` or `InefficientPersonService`, so no finding here names a line I have read.
- **Per-statement baseline.** The baseline's COUNT time split by caller was not read.
- **Gaps in this recording.** There is no `jdk.CPUTimeSample` and no method tracing, so CPU cost by method was not assessed.
